column2: Ajahn Kovilo and Ajahn Nisabho speak with Luang Por Pasanno about dukkha (suffering and unsatisfactoriness), in its personal, social, physical, and psychological aspects.

column6: Session title
Text
Could you describe dukkha? One of your similes that I love relates dukkha to Canadian tires in the wintertime.
Could you describe the difference between the suffering of the three characteristics and the suffering of the Four Noble Truths, the first and second arrows (SN 36.6)?
Chanting Book p. 11: "Birth is dukkha..."

There's a Simon and Garfunkel song that has the line, "Hello darkness, my old friend." I've heard you change the lyrics of that to, "Hello dukkha, my old friend." How far back does your understanding of dukkha go? You talk to some Americans, and they're like, "Dukkha, suffering? I don't have any of that." Looking back, when did you first meet dukkha?
In the most beautiful landscape in the world and still suffering.
When did you first have faith that there was truly a way out?
There's a story about waiting for the afternoon sweet drink all night long (Stillness Flowing p. 504). Was this you?
Ajahn Pasanno's first Pāṭimokkha at Wat Pah Pong.
Ajahn Chah provided the opportunity to reflect about difficulty (Thai _toramon_).
I don't teach wisdom. I just give toramon.|Ajahn Chah
You have lived with intense physical pain for some time due to many injuries. You don't mention it often or show it at all really. What methods do you use to confront that most coarse form of dukkha?
We have the resources within ourselves to not be intimidated by pain or discomfort.

I'm also curious about mental pain. In 1992, you were invited by Ajahn Chah to become the abbot of Wat Pah Nanachat when you were less than ten years in robes. Shortly after, Ajahn Chah became paralyzed and was no longer able to communicate. You took groups of monks every week to pay respects to him, and for ten years were looking after him. Can you explain how you related to that whole mass of dukkha that must have come up? How do you advise others dealing with similar things?

How can you acknowledge the limitations of the personality and of the circumstance but find a deeper wisdom beyond that? For those who find themselves in difficult situations with life and think that release of suffering in this life is beyond them, what thoughts would you offer?

Luang Por Dune reframes the Four Noble Truths. He says the cause of dukkha is ???, sending the mind out, and the result of that is dukkha. The path is ???, the mind seeing the mind, and the fruit of that is the Third Noble Truths, nirodha. Can you say more about this?

The world has real fears in it right now---AI, war, beyond.... What thoughts do you have for people dealing with the suffering of the wider commentary, the news cycle, and real concerns about the shape of politics in the world?
Mv 1.11: “Go out for the welfare and happiness of the manyfolk.”
What about someone who votes and is doing their best to take care of their local community, but they still find their heart darkening with these concerns?
The world has been falling about for a long time. This is not a new phenomenon.
The 30th anniversary of Nature Care.

If I did it with the idea that I've got to protect all the forests in Thailand, I'd just get frustrated. But what I can do is plant seeds for people to protect at least some of it, and that's a good example for other people in the future.

We've already talked about the quote from the Buddha, "Spiritual companionship is the whole of the Holy Life (SN 45.2)." Someone asked you a question about that, and you said, "Living with other people---it's horrible!" And then you laughed a huge Luang Por Pasanno laugh. Could you talk about the paradox that living with other people is half the Holy Life and it's dukkha? You didn't have to be an abbot. You could have lived a hermit's life. Any insights into balancing that?
Is there one teaching of the Buddha or sutta that's rung in you these last years or through your life that stands out more than the others?
MN 30: Cūḷasāropama Sutta (Shorter Heartwood Simile).
Brief ++reflection++ for the Clear Mountain Project: "Don't confuse what's really important."
MN 30: Cūḷasāropama Sutta (Shorter Heartwood Simile).
Having lived in Thailand for over 20 years and in America for 30 years, do you see any American patterns of dukkha, ways that Americans get caught?
I can never get enlightened.|Ajahn Sumedho
The 'I' does not have inherent existence. We have to make it. And then we have to look after it.
When you're not dealing with suffering, where do you reside in your practice or what do you focus on?
Do you have any final advice for two monks in Seattle.
This is just the beginning of your dukkha.
